clue.text: Jeers from New Zealand about Tibetan leader's footwear?

parts.note: the capital city of New Zealand, so what comes from there

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jeers wrap around the letter taken from the Tibetan

parts.note: jeers are boos from a crowd

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so only the opening letter of the word before it is kept

parts.note: the first letter of Tibetan

explanation.surface: Kiwis mock the Dalai Lama's shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jeers from New Zealand' reads as one idea, but it is two pieces: jeers from Wellington, with T inside the BOOS.
explanation.definitionFit: Wellington boots are rubber knee-high boots, a type of footwear named after the Duke of Wellington.

clue.text: Tedious spring event

parts.note: something tedious feels long
to spring is to jump

explanation.surface: A boring springtime occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' suggests the season; here it is a leap.
explanation.definitionFit: The long jump is an athletics competition, one event in a track and field meeting.

clue.text: Restrain youngster crossing river

indicators.note: something crossing another lies across it, so the youngster's letters sit either side of the river's

parts.note: a cub is a young animal, or a junior scout
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Holding a child back as it tries to wade over a river.
explanation.definitionFit: To curb something is to check or hold it back, a straight synonym of restrain.

clue.text: Joint protectors affording Spooner vital rest periods

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the start sounds of the two words get exchanged

parts.note: something vital is key
naps are short rests
swap the opening K and N sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: Pads for the knees that give a sleepy cleric his important siestas.
explanation.walkthrough: KEY NAPS with its first sounds swapped is said 'nee kaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: The kneecap is the bone shielding the front of the knee joint, so kneecaps are joint protectors.

clue.text: Zambia's hyperactive breeze

parts.note: Z is Zambia's international vehicle registration code

indicators.note: active letters are lively and moving about, so the four before them get rearranged

parts.note: the word's first five letters supply the fodder, its tail the shuffle signal

explanation.surface: A frantic wind blowing across Zambia.
explanation.walkthrough: One word does two jobs: 'hyperactive' splits into HYPER and the anagram signal 'active'.
explanation.definitionFit: A zephyr is a gentle, mild wind, originally the west wind in Greek myth.

clue.text: Old codger briefly profits from bloomers

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter of the old codger word is dropped

parts.note: an old crock is a decrepit old person
to profit from something is to use it

explanation.surface: An old man makes a quick buck out of underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' suggests baggy knickers; it means flowering plants.
explanation.definitionFit: Crocuses are spring-flowering bulbs, so they are things that bloom.

clue.text: Settles into bed, regularly doing something immoral

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the word that follows is kept

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of doing
a sin is a wrongful act

explanation.surface: Someone goes to bed with a habit of misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: The bed is a garden bed, not a sleeping place.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig compost in is to work it into the soil of a flower bed, where it settles.

clue.text: Only bright chaps up for election? Henry's included all the same

indicators.note: something included is put inside, so the Henry letter goes into the phrase before it

parts.words: Only bright chaps up for election?
parts.note: if only clever men are candidates, there is no twit standing
the henry is the unit of inductance, symbol H

explanation.surface: An election where only clever men run, with someone called Henry in the mix.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the first part is a cryptic description of the phrase 'no twit standing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Notwithstanding means nevertheless or despite that, an exact synonym of all the same.

clue.text: Persuasive quality of procession heading off round Lesotho's borders

indicators.note: round means going around, so the shortened procession surrounds the edge letters
with its heading off, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a sequence is a series, one thing following another

indicators.note: borders are the edges, so only the outside letters of the country are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of Lesotho

explanation.surface: A parade in southern Africa makes a convincing impression.
explanation.definitionFit: Eloquence is fluent, convincing speech, the quality that makes speaking persuasive.

clue.text: Animal's ready

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a large horned African or Asian beast
second meaning: old British slang for money, as 'the ready' is cash

explanation.walkthrough: Ready looks like an adjective; it is the noun for cash, as in 'ready money'. Rhino is dated British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the thick-skinned beast and, in old slang, cash, which is also called the ready.

clue.text: Such as you can read, say, in appalling libel

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another, here inside the reworked word
appalling means dreadfully bad, so the word after it is mangled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
e.g. (for example) is how one says 'say'

explanation.surface: A dreadful libel at least has the virtue of being readable.
explanation.definitionFit: Legible writing is clear enough to be read, so it is the kind you can read.

clue.text: Drudge went out with useful tool

parts.note: a hack is a drudge doing dull work, especially writing
to see someone is to go out with them romantically

explanation.surface: A put-upon worker leaves the house carrying something handy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went out with' reads as one phrase, but 'with' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacksaw is a fine-toothed saw for cutting metal, a handy workshop implement.

clue.text: Almost worthless intelligence

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut from the phrase

parts.note: something worthless is no use

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on some unreliable spy reports.
explanation.walkthrough: Intelligence suggests secret information; here it means common sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous is practical good sense, a British informal word for intelligence or savvy.

clue.text: Carson's Act unfortunately set aside

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters before it come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A comedian's routine sadly gets dropped from the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set aside' sounds like cancelled; here it means kept apart as holy.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacrosanct things are regarded as sacred, reserved and not to be touched, as if set apart.

clue.text: Headgear for police caught out at junction

parts.note: a T-junction, shaped like the letter

indicators.note: out means leaving, so the letter for caught is removed from the police word

parts.note: coppers is slang for police officers
c is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Police helmets for officers who nabbed someone at a crossroads.
explanation.definitionFit: Toppers are top hats, tall formal hats, so a kind of headgear.

clue.text: Apology for a dance

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a polite phrase saying sorry
second meaning: a dance at which partners may be cut in on

explanation.walkthrough: An excuse-me is a ballroom dance where anyone may take over another's partner by saying the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a polite way of saying sorry, and also the name of a dance where people swap partners.

clue.text: Closes a street in Cambridgeshire region

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside another, here inside the regional word

parts.note: the Fens are the flat marshy lowlands of Cambridgeshire and East Anglia
St is the abbreviation for street
taken as written

explanation.surface: A road shuts somewhere in rural East Anglia.
explanation.definitionFit: To fasten is to secure or shut something, so fastens matches closes as a verb.

clue.text: Feeble female runs away from daredevil

indicators.note: something that runs away leaves, so the runs letter is taken out of the next word

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female
r is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs
a daredevil attitude is reckless

explanation.surface: A timid woman flees from a thrill-seeker.
explanation.walkthrough: Daredevil is used as an adjective here, as in 'daredevil stunts'.
explanation.definitionFit: Feckless means ineffectual and lacking in purpose, close in sense to weak or feeble.

clue.text: Ozzie runners accepting overdue challenges

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the runners hold the overdue word inside

parts.note: emus are fast flightless Australian birds
overdue means late

explanation.surface: Australian athletes taking on challenges that are long overdue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Challenges' looks like a noun; it is a verb meaning rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: To emulate someone is to try to equal or rival them, so emulates means rivals or challenges.

clue.text: Part of church unfinished after a century in recession? No way!

indicators.note: something in recession is going back, so these words are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a ton is a hundred, as a century in cricket

indicators.note: unfinished means lacking its end, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: the chancel is the area around a church's altar

explanation.surface: A church left incomplete for a hundred years of economic slump? Out of the question!
explanation.walkthrough: The church part comes second in the answer though it comes first in the clue, because of 'after'.
explanation.definitionFit: Not a chance is an emphatic refusal or denial, the same idiom as no way.

clue.text: Tremble as examiner's son leaves for Spain

indicators.note: one thing leaving for another means it is swapped out, the son letter replaced by the Spain letter

parts.note: a tester examines things
s is the abbreviation for son
E is Spain's international vehicle code, from España

explanation.surface: A nervous parent watches a child head off to Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: To teeter is to wobble unsteadily, so it is a near synonym of tremble or shake.

clue.text: Gangster with weapons causes anxiety

parts.note: Al Capone, the crossword's stock gangster
arms are weapons

explanation.surface: An armed mobster frightens people.
explanation.definitionFit: To alarm someone is to make them frightened or worried, so alarms is to cause anxiety.

clue.text: Fan backing a swimmer

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the words before it are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a nut is an enthusiast, as in a fitness nut
taken as written

explanation.surface: A supporter cheers on a competitor in the pool.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface links 'Fan backing' as a supporter, but 'a' and the fan are reversed together.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuna is a large fast ocean fish, so a swimmer in crossword terms.

clue.text: Begins espionage activity initially where there are few observers?

parts.note: opens means begins

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letters of the two words before it are used

parts.note: the first letters of espionage and activity

explanation.surface: Spying kicks off somewhere nobody is watching.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a playful definition: out on the open ocean there is hardly anyone to see you, apt for spying.
explanation.definitionFit: The open sea is ocean far from land, where few people are around to watch.

clue.text: Country boy conceals map

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so the boy word wraps around the map word

parts.note: a lad is a boy
a plan is a map or diagram

explanation.surface: A rural lad hides his map.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' looks like an adjective describing the boy, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapland is the Arctic region of the Sami people, loosely a land or country across northern Scandinavia.

clue.text: Work at grasping old manoeuvre

indicators.note: grasping means holding, so the work word holds the old letter inside it

parts.note: to ply a trade is to work at it
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Practising an old trick until it is mastered.
explanation.definitionFit: A ploy is a cunning tactic or stratagem, so it matches a manoeuvre.

clue.text: Session at school containing hospital unit

indicators.note: containing means holding inside, so the session word holds the hospital letter

parts.note: a school year is split into terms
H is the map symbol for hospital

explanation.surface: A school term that includes a spell in the sick bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hospital unit' looks like a ward; the unit is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A therm is a British measure of heat, 100,000 British thermal units, used for gas bills.

clue.text: Given money, corrupt sovereign (not English) might do so

definitions.text: Given money, corrupt sovereign (not English) might do so

indicators.note: corrupt means spoiled or debased, so the letters are thrown into a new order
not means without, so one letter for English is left out of the ruler word

parts.note: m is a common abbreviation for money
taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A bribed and crooked monarch abroad would rule badly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a corrupt king who takes bribes would rule a country badly.
explanation.definitionFit: To misgovern is to rule badly, exactly what a bribed, crooked monarch would be expected to do.
